abstract.title: Abstract
abstract.p: Infectious complications are common following chimeric antigen receptor (CAR) T-cell therapy for B-cell lymphoma due to its prolonged immunosuppressive effects. Schizophyllum commune is an exceedingly rare fungal pathogen that typically affects the respiratory tract and may mimic chronic pulmonary aspergillosis. Infections caused by S. commune have been primarily reported in recipients of allogeneic hematopoietic stem cell transplantation. Here, we report the first known case of S. commune infection in a patient treated with CAR T-cell therapy. A 71-year-old woman with primary refractory large B-cell lymphoma received lisocabtagene maraleucel as second-line therapy. Six months post-treatment, computed tomography revealed right middle lobe atelectasis with high-attenuation mucus. Bronchoscopic biopsy, fungal culture, and internal transcribed spacer gene region sequencing confirmed the diagnosis of S. commune infection presenting as allergic bronchopulmonary mycosis (ABPM). Notably, serologic tests were negative for fungus-specific specific immunoglobulin G and immunoglobulin E. The patient responded favorably to 4 months of oral voriconazole therapy, with resolution of symptoms and radiologic findings. This case highlights the potential for rare fungal infections, such as S. commune, to occur following CAR T-cell therapy. Although the clinical and radiologic features were consistent with ABPM, the absence of serologic markers underscores the diagnostic challenges posed by B-cell aplasia resulting from B-cell-directed immunotherapy.

sec.p: Keywords: Schizophyllum commune, allergic bronchopulmonary mycosis, chimeric antigen receptor T-cell therapy, fungal infection, large B-cell lymphoma

sec.title: INTRODUCTION
sec.p: CD19-directed chimeric antigen receptor (CAR) T-cell therapy has markedly improved the prognosis of patients with relapsed or refractory large B-cell lymphoma (LBCL).1–3 Nevertheless, infectious complications remain a significant concern following CAR T-cell therapy due to its prolonged immunosuppressive effects, which include extended neutropenia, hypogammaglobulinemia, B-cell aplasia, and decreased CD4+T-cell counts.4,5

Schizophyllum commune is a basidiomycetous fungus that is rarely pathogenic in humans.6 Unlike many other fungal pathogens that typically cause invasive fungal infections (IFIs), S. commune frequently presents as allergic bronchopulmonary mycosis (ABPM), particularly in Japan.7 Reported cases of S. commune infection in patients with hematologic malignancies have primarily involved individuals with acute leukemia or those who have undergone allogeneic hematopoietic stem cell transplantation.8–12

Here, we describe the first documented case of pulmonary S. commune infection following CAR T-cell therapy. In such patients, classical diagnostic features of ABPM may be absent or attenuated due to underlying lymphoma or CAR T-cell therapy–associated hypogammaglobulinemia, potentially obscuring serologic markers such as fungus-specific immunoglobulin G (IgG) or immunoglobulin E (IgE).13 Despite these diagnostic limitations, accurate identification can be achieved through bronchoscopic biopsy, fungal culture, and internal transcribed spacer (ITS) gene region sequencing of the isolate. This case underscores the need to consider rare and atypical fungal infections such as S. commune as potential late-onset complications in patients receiving CAR T-cell therapy.

sec.title: CASE REPORT
sec.p: A 71-year-old woman with a history of primary refractory LBCL was referred to our institution for CAR T-cell therapy. She had been diagnosed with LBCL 14 months earlier and initially received six cycles of polatuzumab vedotin, rituximab, cyclophosphamide, doxorubicin, and prednisolone (Pola-R-CHP). However, disease progression was observed despite treatment. She subsequently received lisocabtagene maraleucel as second-line therapy. Three months after CAR T-cell infusion, positron emission tomography-computed tomography (PET-CT) showed a complete metabolic response. However, a follow-up PET-CT scan at 6 months revealed abnormal fluorodeoxyglucose uptake along the pleura of the right middle lobe, with a maximum standardized uptake value of 15.02.(Fig. 1). Concurrently, the patient developed a persistent cough, initially attributed to allergic rhinitis and empirically managed with oral antihistamines at a local clinic.

caption.p: PET-CT on day 180 after CAR T-cell infusion.
(A) MIP image.
(B) Axial view showing a lesion along the pleura of the right middle lobe.
(C) Increased FDG uptake at the lesion margin, with an SUVmax of 15.02.

Abbreviations: PET-CT, positron emission tomography–computed tomography; MIP, maximum intensity projection; FDG, fluorodeoxyglucose; SUVmax, maximum standardized uptake value; CAR, chimeric antigen receptor.

sec.p: Her medical history included type 2 diabetes mellitus and dyslipidemia. She had no prior history of asthma, smoking, or respiratory infections. She lived in an urban area with limited exposure to forested environments or soil. On physical examination, vital signs were stable, and no abnormalities were noted on chest auscultation or systemic examination. She remained afebrile and maintained adequate oxygen saturation levels throughout the post-CAR T-cell therapy period.

Laboratory evaluation at 6 months post-infusion revealed mild eosinophilia (740/μL) and hypogammaglobulinemia, including reduced levels of IgG (407 mg/dL), immunoglobulin A (IgA 21 mg/dL), immunoglobulin M (IgM 40 mg/dL), and IgE (3 IU/mL). C-reactive protein (CRP) was slightly elevated (0.17 mg/dL). Inflammatory markers and fungal antigens, including serum β-D-glucan and galactomannan, were negative. Selected laboratory results are presented in Table 1. Serial trends in peripheral blood cell counts following CAR T-cell infusion are shown in Fig. 2. Grade 4 neutropenia developed on day 14 post-infusion and resolved with administration of granulocyte colony-stimulating factor, initiated on day 15 and continued until day 88 to maintain an absolute neutrophil count above 1000/µL. The duration of Grade 4 neutropenia was limited to 2 days. Eosinophilia emerged around day 100, while persistent hypogammaglobulinemia developed approximately 2 months after infusion. CD4+ T-cell counts remained above 200/µL throughout follow-up, whereas B-cell aplasia persisted. Notably, the patient did not experience cytokine release syndrome (CRS), immune effector cell-associated neurotoxicity syndrome (ICANS), or any other treatment-related adverse events. No additional infectious episodes were documented during the post-infusion period.

The clinical timeline indicates the day of CAR T-cell infusion and tracks longitudinal changes in neutrophil count, eosinophil count, CD4+ T-cell count, CD19+B-cell count, and IgG levels.

sec.p: Chest CT at 6 months post-CAR T-cell therapy revealed atelectasis of the right middle lobe, characterized by central bronchiectasis and high-attenuation mucus impaction, without evidence of a mass lesion (Figs. 3A–C). Bronchoscopy revealed obstruction of the right middle lobe bronchus (segments B4+5) by thick, yellowish mucus (Figs. 3D–F). The mucus was suctioned, resulting in airway reopening, and forceps biopsy samples were obtained.

caption.p: Chest CT and bronchoscopic findings.

(A–C) CT images show right middle lobe atelectasis, central bronchiectasis, and high-attenuation mucus (arrow) within the bronchial lumen. No discrete tumorous lesion was noted in the area of FDG uptake on PET-CT.
(D) Bronchoscopic image revealing pale yellow mucus obstructing the right middle lobe bronchus (segments B4+5).
(E) Mucus plug removed by suction.
(F) Reopening of the right B4+5 bronchus following mucus removal.
Abbreviations: CT, computed tomography; PET-CT, positron emission tomography–computed tomography; FDG, fluorodeoxyglucose.

sec.p: Histopathological examination of the bronchial biopsy demonstrated eosinophilic inflammation and necrotic debris. Grocott methenamine silver staining revealed the presence of fungal hyphae (Figs. 4A, B). Gram staining of bronchoalveolar lavage fluid was negative for bacteria. On day 8 of fungal culture, growth consistent with filamentous fungi was observed. By day 18, white, cottony colonies appeared on Sabouraud dextrose chloramphenicol gentamicin agar (Fig. 4C). Clamp connections were not observed. Matrix-assisted laser desorption/ionization time-of-flight mass spectrometry (MALDI-TOF MS) identified the organism as S. commune with a score value of 2.19. ITS gene region sequencing of the isolate further confirmed the diagnosis. Despite these microbiological findings, enzyme-linked immunosorbent assay for S. commune–specific antibodies was negative: the IgG antibody concentration was 0.0390 mg/dL (reference: <0.1387 mg/dL) and the IgE level was 0.0275 mg/dL (reference: <0.1034 mg/dL).

caption.p: Histopathological and microbiological findings.
(A) H&E staining (×600): infiltration of eosinophils and mucus-rich tissue, and presence of Charcot–Leyden crystals, consistent with eosinophilic inflammation.
(B) GMS staining (×600): filamentous fungal hyphae observed within necrotic tissue.
(C) Fungal culture on day 18: white, cottony colonies of Schizophyllum commune grown on Sabouraud dextrose chloramphenicol gentamicin agar.
Abbreviations: H&E, hematoxylin and eosin; GMS, Grocott methenamine silver

sec.p: Due to the negative serologic results, the patient did not fulfill the International Society for Human and Animal Mycology (ISHAM) diagnostic criteria for allergic bronchopulmonary aspergillosis (ABPA).14 Nevertheless, based on the clinical presentation, radiologic features, microbiologic evidence, and histopathological findings, a diagnosis of S. commune pulmonary infection presenting as ABPM was made. The patient was treated with oral voriconazole for 4 months. Follow-up CT imaging showed complete resolution of the pulmonary lesion (Fig. 5), and peripheral eosinophil count declined to below 500/µL. Serum β-D-glucan remained negative throughout the treatment course.

caption.p: Changes in chest CT findings following antifungal therapy.
(A) CT before treatment.
(B) CT after 2 months of oral voriconazole therapy.
(C) CT at the end of 4 months of treatment, showing resolution of atelectasis and improvement in bronchial abnormalities.
Abbreviations: CT, computed tomography.

sec.title: DISCUSSION
sec.p: To the best of our knowledge, this is the first reported case of S. commune infection in a patient with lymphoma treated with CAR T-cell therapy. This case provides two key insights. First, patients receiving CAR T-cell therapy may enter an immunocompromised state comparable to that seen in recipients of allogeneic hematopoietic stem cell transplantation, thereby increasing susceptibility to opportunistic infections such as S. commune. Second, diagnosing S. commune infection in the context of B-cell aplasia can be particularly challenging, especially in CAR T-cell recipients.

Five previously documented cases of S. commune infection in patients with hematologic malignancies have been reported, as summarized in Table 2.8–12 These infections occurred under conditions of profound immunosuppression, most commonly after allogeneic hematopoietic stem cell transplantation or intensive chemotherapy, such as induction therapy for acute myeloid leukemia. Notably, no prior cases have been reported in patients with non-Hodgkin lymphoma.

sec.p: When evaluating fungal infections following CAR T-cell therapy, it is important to recognize that neutropenia may persist after lymphodepleting chemotherapy as well as post-infusion, though its duration varies across individuals.15 While the overall incidence of fungal infections following CAR T-cell therapy is considered relatively low,16 real-world data suggest that Aspergillus and Candida species are the most commonly identified fungal pathogens, affecting approximately 1–9% of CAR T-cell recipients within the first 30 days post-infusion.17 However, most studies focus on early-onset fungal infections, and reports of on late-onset infections remain scarce, with an incidence of less than 1%.16,18,19 Several risk factors have been proposed for fungal infections in this setting, including prolonged neutropenia (lasting >14 days), severe CRS or ICANS, prolonged corticosteroid use (>72 hr), mechanical ventilation, prior allogeneic hematopoietic stem cell transplantation, and a history of fungal infections.18,20 Although our patient did not have classical risk factors for invasive fungal disease, persistent hypogammaglobulinemia may have contributed to susceptibility. Immunoglobulin replacement therapy has been reported to reduce infection risk in patients with B-cell aplasia following CAR T-cell therapy,21 although its role in preventing fungal infections requires further study. This case underscores that invasive fungal infections can develop in CAR T-cell recipients even in the absence of established risk factors. In such patients, assessing the degree of immunocompromise remains challenging. Although peripheral immune cell counts, such as neutrophils and lymphocytes, are readily available, functional and phenotypic assessments of immune cells are not routinely feasible in clinical settings. This highlights the need for more comprehensive immunological evaluations to better stratify infection risk and guide prophylactic strategies in this population.

S. commune is a representative species of the Schizophyllaceae family, order Agaricales, phylum Basidiomycota. It is a saprophytic fungus commonly found on decaying wood and is widely distributed worldwide, including in Japan.22 Infections caused by S. commune, collectively referred to as Schizophyllum mycosis, most frequently manifest as allergic ABPM—a hypersensitivity-mediated airway disease driven by type I and type III immune responses to fungal elements within the bronchial tree. A nationwide surveillance study of 358 ABPM cases in Japan identified S. commune as the causative organism in 21 cases (6%), confirming its role as a rare but recognized pathogen.23 ABPM is typically diagnosed using the ISHAM-ABPA criteria for ABPA (2024),14 although in Japan, the criteria established by the Japanese ABPM Working Group (2021) are also widely applied.24 In the present case, although fungus-specific IgE and total serum IgE—two essential components of the ISHAM criteria—were not elevated, several other features were compatible with ABPM, including peripheral eosinophilia, positive fungal culture from bronchoalveolar lavage fluid, and thin-section CT findings of central bronchiectasis, mucus plugging and high-attenuation mucus (HAM). HAM is particularly important, as it is considered a pathognomonic feature for ABPM.14 Low total serum IgE and negative fungus-specific IgE and IgG are uncommon in ABPM but have been reported in patients with cystic fibrosis and ABPA.25–27

Among patients with B-cell lymphoma undergoing B-cell-targeted therapies—such as CD19-targeted CAR T-cell therapy or CD20-directed bispecific antibody therapy—prolonged B-cell aplasia may impair the generation of pathogen-specific antibodies, thereby complicating serologic diagnosis. This immunodeficiency can lead to false-negative results in conventional serologic assays, complicating diagnosis. B-cell depletion following these therapies is known to significantly affect the accuracy of serological tests for infections, and hypogammaglobulinemia is recognized as a risk factor for infections.13,21 Therefore, clinicians should interpret serologic test results with caution in these patients and consider alternative diagnostic methods.

Even in the setting of B-cell depletion, it is known that cytokine production by Th2 cells—particularly interleukin (IL)-4 and IL-5—can induce ABPM-like responses by promoting tissue inflammation and eosinophilic recruitment at local sites.28

Although the ISHAM criteria were not fully met, the patient fulfilled six diagnostic components established by the Japanese ABPM Working Group: (1) peripheral eosinophilia (>500 cells/mm3); (2) growth of filamentous fungi in sputum or bronchial lavage fluid cultures; (3) presence of fungal hyphae in bronchial mucus plugs; (4) central bronchiectasis on chest CT; (5) visible mucus plugs in central bronchi as confirmed by CT, bronchoscopy, or clinical; and (6) high-attenuation mucus in bronchi on CT imaging. Based on these criteria, a diagnosis of ABPM was established.

The optimal treatment strategy for S. commune remains unclear due to the rarity of the infection. Oral corticosteroids are generally recommended for ABPM.22 While corticosteroids significantly reduce recurrence risk, the role of antifungal therapy remains debated. Nonetheless, itraconazole and voriconazole are frequently used in clinical practice for ABPM,14,29,30 and liposomal amphotericin B has been occasionally administered in S. commune infections among patients with hematologic malignancies (Table2).8–12 Because of its rarity, there have been no comprehensive reports on the treatment of Schizophyllum commune infection. However, Research that summarized the management of allergic bronchopulmonary mycosis (ABPM) in Japan told oral corticosteroids, antifungal agents, and anti-IgE antibodies (omalizumab) were widely used. The most common regimen was combined treatment with oral corticosteroids and antifungal agents (46%), followed by corticosteroids alone (75%) and antifungal agents alone (10%). Antifungal agents were used in 56% of cases overall. These patterns differ somewhat from the treatment strategies reported for hematologic malignancies described above. Given the lack of comprehensive data on the management of S. commune infection, the therapeutic approach used in our case may not be universally effective.22 In the present case, corticosteroids were avoided due to the patient’s history of CAR T-cell therapy and underlying diabetes mellitus. Antifungal monotherapy with voriconazole was selected. Notably, corticosteroid use following CAR T-cell therapy may impair therapeutic efficacy,31 necessitating cautious consideration in this population. Accordingly, antifungal monotherapy may be a reasonable and effective alternative for ABPM in selected patients receiving immunotherapy, such as CAR T-cell therapy or bispecific antibodies.

In conclusion, we report the first documented case of pulmonary S. commune infection following CAR T-cell therapy in a patient with LBCL. Clinical and radiologic findings were consistent with ABPM. In the absence of elevated IgE or S. commune–specific antibodies, this case highlights the diagnostic challenges of ABPM among patients with B-cell lymphoma with persistent B-cell aplasia due to B-cell-targeting immunotherapy.
